title: Hashing.consistentHash() allocates a new object on every call
body:
Guava Version
33.6.0-jre
Description
I was building a load balancer that routes incoming requests to backend shards using consistent hashing. My hot path calls Hashing.consistentHash(hashCode, numBuckets) for every request — several thousand times per second under normal traffic.
While profiling with async-profiler, I noticed a steady stream of LinearCongruentialGenerator allocations showing up in the allocation flamegraph, all originating from consistentHash. I dug into the source and found that every single call to consistentHash allocates a new LinearCongruentialGenerator object. That class holds exactly one long field. There is no reason for it to be a heap-allocated object at all — the field and the arithmetic it performs could be local variables inside consistentHash itself.
Under heavy traffic this generates constant GC pressure for no gain. Inlining the single field and the formula from nextDouble() directly into consistentHash would make the allocation disappear entirely with zero behavioral change.
Relevant source: Hashing.java line 657, LinearCongruentialGenerator inner class lines 825–836.
How to reproduce:
Run the following code and attach an allocation profiler (e.g., async-profiler with -e alloc, or JVM flag -Xlog:gc to watch minor GC frequency):
HashCode hash = Hashing.murmur3_128().hashLong(42L);
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; i++) {
Hashing.consistentHash(hash, 100);
}
Observe LinearCongruentialGenerator objects appearing in the allocation profile at a rate of one per consistentHash call.
Alternatively, open Hashing.java and inspect line 657 — a new LinearCongruentialGenerator(input) allocation appears unconditionally on every call path.
Example
Example: Imagine a postal sorting facility that assigns each incoming letter to one of 100 bins using a fixed formula written on a reference card. For every single letter, instead of using the same card on the desk, a worker takes a blank sheet, hand-writes the formula on it, uses it once, and throws it away. The formula never changes — writing a new sheet for every letter is pure waste. The formula should just live on the desk as a few local variables, ready to use for the next letter the moment the current one is sorted.
Expected Behavior

consistentHash computes and returns the correct bucket index using only stack-allocated local variables.
No heap objects are allocated per call beyond the method frame itself.
Under high call frequency the method contributes zero allocation pressure to the GC.

Actual Behavior

A new LinearCongruentialGenerator instance is heap-allocated on every single call, regardless of call frequency.
Under high throughput (e.g., thousands of calls per second) this generates a continuous stream of short-lived objects, increasing minor GC frequency and adding measurable latency spikes in allocation-profiler traces.

com.google.common.hash

Prepare Guava for JEP 500 ("Prepare to Make Final Mean Final")
body:
The problem I'm aware of at the moment is with Serialization.getFieldSetter. It is used from:

ConcurrentHashMultiset
ImmutableMultimap
ImmutableSetMultimap
TreeMultiset

I hacked up pom.xml to have its Surefire argLine  contain --illegal-final-field-mutation=deny. Then I grabbed a jdk-26-ea+25, configured it as a <version>26-ea</version> in my .m2/toolchains.xml (because it needs to be "configured," not just "discovered"), and ran tests with it (in a victory for c171b9c):
$ JAVA_HOME=/usr/local/google/home/cpovirk/jdk-26-ea+25 ./mvnw clean install -Dmaven.javadoc.skip -Dtoolchain.skip -Dsurefire.toolchain.version=26-ea
The resulting failures are many (over 10k), but that's because our test-suite builders attempt to perform a huge number of tests on reserialized collections, so a deserialization failure breaks them all. All the failures trace to three fields:

AbstractSortedMultiset.comparator
ConcurrentHashMultiset.countMap
ImmutableMultimap.map

I think the four hits from my Serialization.getFieldSetter search are more accurate: The code fails at runtime on the first field that it tries to set, so we don't get far enough to see the field specific to ImmutableSetMultimap.

A suggestion of code improvement for BloomFilter.
body:
API(s)
com.google.common.hash.BloomFilter::optimalNumOfBits(long n, double p)
&
com.google.common.hash.BloomFilter::optimalNumOfHashFunctions(long n, long m)
How do you want it to be improved?
1. use static caculated value of log(2)  and squared log(2) :
        private static final double LOG_TWO = Math.log(2);
	private static final double SQUARED_LOG_TWO = Math.pow(LOG_TWO,2);
2. calculate optimalNumOfBits by static values:
	static long optimalNumOfBits(long n, double p) {
	    if (p == 0) {
			p = Double.MIN_VALUE;
	    }
	    return (long) (-n * Math.log(p) / SQUARED_LOG_TWO);
	}
3. caculate optimalNumOfHashFunction by false positive rate(p) directly and using LOG_TWO :
     	static int optimalNumOfHashFunctions(double p){
		return  Math.max(1, (int) Math.round( - Math.log(p) / LOG_TWO));
	}
Why do we need it to be improved?

Slightly reduce the method's execution time.
Refine the calculation of the optimalNumOfHashFunctions method to be more concise and efficient. The current code may lead people to mistakenly believe that the result is related to the number of samples(n) and the number of bits（m）, when in fact it is only related to the false positive rate(p).

body:
Every now and then I'd like to check a variable for a non-null value or otherwise provide a reasonable non-null default value. Sometimes the second value is computed or should be created on-demand for different reasons. Therefore please provide
T firstNonNull(T first, Supplier<? extends T> second) for that.
firstNonNull is much more concise and expressive than requireNonNullElseGet or Optional.ofNullable(first).orElseGet(() -> second()).
Additionally: java.util.Objects.requireNonNullElseGet(T obj, Supplier<? extends T> supplier) should be mentioned in Javadoc as an alternative for incoming parameter validation.
Thank you for your great library.

title: Make `Iterators.mergeSorted()` stable
body:
I've noticed that Iterators.mergeSorted() is unstable.
So for example if I have arrays: [A_1, B_1, C_1] [A_2, B_2, C_2] (where the comparator looks only at the letter), I'd like the result to iterate [A_1, A_2,  B_1, B_2,  C_1, C_2]. The current implementation doesn't guarantee this.
Might it be possible to add a stable version?
I confess it's not obvious what to do if the arrays are something like [A_1, A_2, B_1], [A_3] - to me it would make sense to empty the first iterator of A_n elements before moving on to the second, so [A_1, A_2, A_3, B_1].
[I appreciate I'm being a little lazy with my terminology here - I can provide a fully fleshed example if it's not clear]

title: Halve memory used by BloomFilter.java : readFrom()
body:
guava/src/com/google/common/hash/BloomFilter.java
readFrom allocates a temporary bitmap (data) of the size required, fills it and then passes that to new LockFreeBitArray(data) which allocates the same amount of memory and copies the bitmap (data) which is then discarded.
If the bitmap (data) is say 100MB in size, then double that of memory used during this process (along with extra CPU in the copy).
The readFrom could allocate the LockFreeBitArray(data) itself and read the data directly into that bitmap instead of using a temporary intermediate bitmap.
